title: The 10 Biggest Days in AI History
dek: On the morning Anthropic begins trading as the biggest IPO in history, NLW looks back at ten days that shaped generative AI. The list runs from OpenAI's founding to the transformer paper, ChatGPT, the Altman ouster, DeepSeek, the agentic turn, Washington's clash with Anthropic and the data-center midterms. It ends with the shift from AI's private era to its public one.

oneIdea.headline: Anthropic's IPO ends AI's private era and starts its public one.
oneIdea.summary: Generative AI's biggest days so far have mostly happened inside private companies. A nonprofit founded out of fear of Google, a transformer paper Google underused, a chatbot Anthropic sat on, a boardroom coup, a model that made agents real. Along the way the public kept pushing in: through Nvidia's crash on DeepSeek, through Washington's fights with Anthropic, and through a midterm vote against data centers. With Anthropic now public, ordinary people can buy into AI's builders directly and those builders face a new degree of transparency. What happens on day one matters much less than what comes next.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: A history lesson with little for the consulting room
items.body: This edition is a retrospective, so it has limited clinical relevance. The one thread worth pulling is that the model families behind most NHS scribes, from Anthropic and OpenAI, are now run by companies under public or political scrutiny they did not face two years ago. NLW counts that as progress; Zitron thinks the scrutiny has come late.

items.title: A model can be withdrawn overnight
items.body: One of the ten days is the eighteen days in June when Anthropic pulled a model for everyone after a government directive. A clinical tool built on a single model can lose it without warning. Ask a scribe supplier which model it depends on, whether it has a fallback, and how a practice would be told if the underlying model changed.

items.title: Pension funds and the AI trade
items.body: Both men note how much of the stock market now rests on AI. That includes funded pension schemes, private pensions and most index trackers. It is not a reason to act, only to recognise that the bubble argument is not somebody else's problem. Neither commentator is a financial adviser, and nor am I.

the_other_side.text: Zitron, in a paid piece published the day after of which only the opening is free to read, offers the opposite history. Where Whittemore lists milestones, Zitron describes a bubble inflated by a press willing to believe any large number from a large company, and says questioning Anthropic's profitability or failing to be excited about its flotation is treated as bad faith. He calls bubble boosterism "an act of cowardice" and writes that the bubble has not yet burst but is clearly on the way. The free section does not discuss the first day's trading.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether a public listing exposes an AI company to scrutiny or simply widens the pool of people exposed to it. Both accept as fact that Anthropic has listed, that ordinary investors can now buy in directly, and that the industry's fortunes are tied to the wider economy. The empirical question is whether public reporting confirms or undermines the business; the observable is Anthropic's first audited quarterly results and how the shares trade once early holders may sell. The residue is worldview: whether the last decade is a record of breakthroughs or of credulity. For Whittemore to be vindicated, disclosure must show demand strong enough that scrutiny helps the company. For Zitron, the filings must show costs outrunning revenue and the shares fall below the offer price. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both think one bad quarter could ripple widely. Watch the first quarterly report and the end of the lock-up period.

headlines.headline: Anthropic IPO day is the start of a very new era
headlines.summary: Anthropic's first day of trading makes it officially the biggest IPO in history. NLW calls it the culmination of many AI storylines, which is why it's the right moment to look back at the other days that got us here.

headlines.headline: OpenAI was founded out of fear of Google
headlines.summary: OpenAI launched as a nonprofit on December 11, 2015. Sam Altman's pitch to Elon Musk was that AI would be built anyway, so it shouldn't be Google that got there first. Musk had already put about $5 million into DeepMind partly to keep an eye on Demis Hassabis. Backers committed a headline $1 billion to advancing digital intelligence 'unconstrained by a need to generate financial return.'

headlines.headline: The nonprofit constraint broke almost immediately
headlines.summary: NLW pairs the founding with June 22, 2019, when OpenAI announced a $1 billion investment from Microsoft. OpenAI had concluded it couldn't raise enough as a nonprofit and created a for-profit arm. That move set off many of the fights that came later.

headlines.headline: Google invented the transformer, and OpenAI saw what it was
headlines.summary: On June 12, 2017, Google Brain published 'Attention Is All You Need,' introducing the architecture behind modern LLMs. Google mostly applied it to search queries and Translate, while OpenAI quickly recognized it as what they'd been looking for. Co-author Noam Shazeer later left Google in 2021 to found Character.ai after Google refused to release his transformer chatbot, Meena.

headlines.headline: Anthropic had a chatbot first, and a rumor about it triggered ChatGPT
headlines.summary: In February 2022, Anthropic was already testing an internal chatbot called Claude but held it back for fear of starting an arms race. That November, OpenAI was preparing GPT-4 when a rumor spread that Anthropic was about to ship a chatbot. OpenAI rushed out its own, announcing it to the team on November 17 and shipping on November 30.

headlines.headline: The team expected tens of thousands of users; they got a million in five days
headlines.summary: Most of OpenAI expected ChatGPT to reach the low tens of thousands of users, and Sam Altman's most optimistic guess was an eventual million. It hit a million in five days and 100 million in five weeks, becoming the fastest-growing application of all time. ChatGPT quickly became synonymous with AI.

headlines.headline: The four-day coup that made OpenAI look beatable
headlines.summary: On November 17, 2023, OpenAI's board fired Sam Altman for not being 'consistently candid,' and never clearly explained what that meant. Interim CEOs changed twice and Microsoft offered to rebuild the team in-house. Almost all of OpenAI's roughly 800 employees threatened to leave, and by November 29 Altman was officially back with a new board.

headlines.headline: The real legacy of the Altman saga: Microsoft started hedging
headlines.summary: NLW argues the drama changed the industry's structure. OpenAI no longer looked unassailable, and the returning Altman was never going to be as powerful as before. Microsoft's access to OpenAI models ended whenever the board declared AGI, which looked much scarier after this episode. That set in motion the Mustafa Suleyman hire and Microsoft's slow move away from OpenAI.

headlines.headline: Claude 3.5 Sonnet was the day Anthropic stepped out of OpenAI's shadow
headlines.summary: On June 20, 2024, Claude 3.5 Sonnet broke new ground in agentic coding and let Cursor, Replit and Lovable bring that capability to non-coders. From then on, Claude models basically led on coding. Coding turned out to be the foundational use case that many other use cases were built on.

headlines.headline: DeepSeek erased $589 billion of Nvidia in one day
headlines.summary: On January 27, 2025, fears about a Chinese lab sent Nvidia down 17%, the biggest one-day loss for any company ever. The panic rested on a viral claim that R1 was trained for $5.5 million, a figure that turned out to be wildly overstated. DeepSeek's free app was also number one on the App Store.

headlines.headline: Most people's first reasoning model came from China
headlines.summary: R1 wasn't the best model in the world; it was a reasoning model like OpenAI's o1. Almost no one had used o1, which spent months in preview and then sat behind paid plans. Nvidia recovered, but the DeepSeek moment changed how Western labs released models and started the US-versus-China framing that has shaped policy ever since.

headlines.headline: Opus 4.5 made the agentic dream real
headlines.summary: Agents were all over the discourse in 2024 and 2025 but not really real until Anthropic released Claude Opus 4.5 on November 24, 2025. It took the community about a month, and some holiday downtime, to realize how different it was. NLW credits the pairing of Opus 4.5 with Claude Code as the true accelerant.

headlines.headline: From Clawdbot to Molt to OpenClaw in a single frenetic week
headlines.summary: Peter Steinberger's open-source agent Clawdbot felt like the first agent that could actually do things for you. Anthropic sent a cease and desist over the name, so it became Molt, and an entrepreneur launched Moltbook, a social network where agents pondered consciousness, griped about users and started a religion. On January 30 the project settled on its final name, OpenClaw, and the agent craze went global.

headlines.headline: Genuinely the most incredible sci-fi takeoff adjacent thing I have recently seen.
headlines.summary: Many Moltbook posts may have been humans posing as agents, or agents role-playing consciousness. It still caught enormous attention as a vision of what the future might look like.

headlines.headline: Agents broke Wall Street's bubble math
headlines.summary: In fall 2025, the AI-bubble fear came down to arithmetic: $20 or $30 seats times the number of available workers didn't add up to the giant infrastructure deals. Once individual agentic users were spending hundreds or thousands of dollars a month, the industry's whole financial picture changed. NLW's view is that Claude Code, Opus 4.5 and OpenClaw together split AI into a pre-agentic and an agentic world.

headlines.headline: The first US company ever labeled a supply chain risk
headlines.summary: On February 27, President Trump ordered federal agencies to stop using Anthropic, and Defense Secretary Hegseth barred it from military use. The trigger was Anthropic's pushback over its models being used in the January raid on Maduro. Its red lines were no autonomous weapons control and no domestic surveillance. Anthropic is still fighting the designation in court.

headlines.headline: The end of labs shipping models whenever they choose
headlines.summary: Anthropic gave its powerful Mythos model a private period under Project Glasswing, letting partners use it to harden systems before public release. After the public version launched in June, Amazon warned the government about a jailbreak. A June 12 directive ordered access cut for foreign nationals, and because Anthropic couldn't build identity checks in time, it pulled the model for everyone for 18 days.

headlines.headline: The midterms became a referendum on data centers
headlines.summary: Backlash built all year over noise, tax breaks, electricity prices, water use and NDAs, and a May Gallup poll found more opposition to a local data center than to a nuclear plant. On November 3, 56% of voters told NBC that data centers were a major or crucial factor in their vote. The pro side lost 45 of 46 local measures, and Democrats flipped both chambers.

headlines.headline: Not a ban hammer, but a demand for a voice
headlines.summary: NLW expects stricter standards and processes rather than a shutdown, and still thinks data centers will get built. He calls it an extremely winnable issue for everyone. The bigger signal, he argues, is that people showed they won't let the future of AI be written without them.

headlines.headline: The real significance: AI goes from private to public
headlines.summary: Anthropic priced on November 18 at $83, above its $70–78 range. People can now invest in AI's builders directly rather than through proxies like semiconductors, and being public forces more transparency. One bad quarter of AI demand could ripple through an economy this tied to AI, but NLW thinks being public is one of the best ways for outsiders to gain influence over these companies.

headlines.headline: ChatGPT might not have gone as far without Stable Diffusion
headlines.summary: The first honorable mention is August 22, 2022, when Stable Diffusion went live. AI-generated images flooding social media helped fuel the late-2022 AI moment alongside ChatGPT.

headlines.headline: o1-preview answered the plateau question
headlines.summary: For much of 2024, the worry was that training methods had hit a wall, which had big implications for AI's disruption and business model. OpenAI's o1-preview on September 12, 2024 showed that reasoning models could squeeze much more out of existing approaches without a new pre-training breakthrough.

headlines.headline: Two dates that sum up the AI trade and the build-out
headlines.summary: Nvidia's May 24, 2023 earnings call began a pattern of the company redefining quarterly performance that continues today. Project Stargate's White House announcement on January 21, 2025, with Altman, Ellison and Son, got the infrastructure story rolling, even though bigger deals have followed.

headlines.headline: Jensen Huang's resignation is the top contender to join this list
headlines.summary: Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on November 12, 2026. It could reshape AI financing given Nvidia's role as the industry's central bank, along with AI policy advocacy and US-China relations. It could also turn out to be a nothing burger, but NLW calls it the likeliest date to climb into the top 10 in a year or two.
